newsitem.title: INDIA: India inferno kills at least 176 Hindu devotees.
newsitem.headline: India inferno kills at least 176 Hindu devotees.

text.p: The death toll in a fire that engulfed a gathering of Hindu worshippers in eastern India has risen to at least 176, and scores of people were missing, authorities said on Monday.
A total of 165 injured were taken to the district hospital, authorities said.

Police in Baripada town, 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital of Orissa state, Bhubaneshwar, said 154 devotees were burnt alive on Sunday when flames tore through bamboo and straw shelters. Another 22 died later in hospital, they said.
Officials at the camp ground, located on a football ground, said some 300 other people from among the 15,000 who had attended the convention were missing.

The inferno swept through a cluster of makeshift shelters on the last day of a convention dedicated to a Hindu guru. All the victims were believed to be male. The cause of the fire was thought to be a short circuit or gas cylinder that exploded.

News agencies said unofficial reports put the death toll at "The scene looked like people were roasted alive on a battlefield," said Amarendra Bose, a resident who visited the site. "The bodies were so mutilated that they were beyond recognition."
The Orissa home (interior) secretary, S.C. Hota, said strong winds fanned the fire, which broke out at about 3:30 p.m. (1000 GMT) on Sunday.
The raging blaze swiftly engulfed eight makeshift huts in the camp at Baripada, 175 km (110 miles) southwest of Calcutta, he said.

"It was a ghastly scene," Bose said. "People with serious burn injuries were being carried off in ambulances. It was a chaotic situation, with people running helter skelter to know the fate of the delegates. Bodies were lying here and there."
Most of the victims were men napping after lunch at the annual national convention, dedicated to the memory of the Hindu guru Nigamananda, Hota said.
"The number of exits at the camp was very limited," Hota said. "That was a problem."
Two fire tenders at the camp were pressed into service but were unable to contain the raging flames, he said. The state government ordered an administrative inquiry into the fire.

"The makeshift houses were completely burned down, reduced to ashes," Bose said, adding that straw had been spread on the ground to serve as bedding. The temperature in the region was 32 degrees Celsius (90 Fahrenheit) and the weather was dry.

Women and children attending the convention which began last Thursday were in 10 huts in a separate area of the camp, authorities said. Residents said the convention's concluding ceremony had been set for later on Sunday.
"The only good thing was that the females' camp was not affected by the fire," Bose said.
The state government said it had ordered the payment of 25,000 rupees ($700) to each of the victims' families and 10,000 rupees ($280) to the seriously injured.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda planned to fly to the site on Monday, his spokesman said.

It was believed to be the deadliest fire in India since about 425 people, mostly children, died when a blaze ripped through a school prize-giving ceremony in the northern town of Dabwali in December 1995.
